title: Pointers
summary: A **pointer** holds the memory address of a value rather than the value itself. Use `&` to take an address and `*` to read or write through it. Pointers let functions modify their caller's data and let you avoid copying large values — without C-style pointer arithmetic.

subtopics.title: & and * : address and dereference
subtopics.explanation: &x produces a pointer to x (its address). If p is a *int, then *p reads the value at that address, and *p = 5 writes through it. The type *T means 'pointer to a T'.
subtopics.example:
x := 10
p := &x   // p is *int
*p = 20   // x is now 20

subtopics.title: The nil pointer & its zero value
subtopics.explanation: The zero value of any pointer type is nil — it points at nothing. Dereferencing a nil pointer panics at runtime, so check for nil before using a pointer that might be unset.
subtopics.example:
var p *int    // nil
if p != nil { fmt.Println(*p) }

subtopics.title: Pass by pointer to mutate
subtopics.explanation: Go is pass-by-value, so a function gets copies of its arguments. Passing a pointer lets the function reach back and modify the caller's value, because the copied pointer still holds the same address.
subtopics.example:
func inc(p *int) { *p++ }
n := 1; inc(&n) // n is 2

subtopics.title: Pointer receivers
subtopics.explanation: A method with a pointer receiver (func (s *T) M()) can modify the value it is called on and avoids copying T. Go automatically takes the address for you: on an addressable value, s.M() becomes (&s).M().

subtopics.title: new() vs &T{}
subtopics.explanation: new(T) allocates a zeroed T and returns a *T. &T{...} allocates a T initialized with a literal and returns its address. Both give you a pointer to heap- or stack-allocated memory (the compiler decides via escape analysis); &T{} is more common because it can initialize fields.

foundations.overview: A pointer is simply the address of a value in memory. With & you take a value's address and with * you follow that address to read or write the value it points to. Pointers are how Go lets a function change its caller's data and how it avoids copying large structs. Unlike C, Go has no pointer arithmetic and a garbage collector tracks what's reachable, so pointers are safe to use.
foundations.formalDefinition: A pointer is a value whose type is *T and whose contents are the memory address of a value of type T. The zero value of every pointer type is nil.
foundations.whyItMatters: Pointers are the mechanism behind mutation across function boundaries, efficient passing of large values, and pointer receivers on methods — all foundational to writing real Go.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of a value as a house and a pointer as a slip of paper with the house's street address. Copying the slip (the pointer) is cheap and still leads everyone to the same house; '*' means 'go to that address and look inside.'
foundations.runtimePerspective: A pointer is a single machine word (8 bytes on 64-bit). The compiler's escape analysis decides whether the pointed-to value lives on the stack (freed automatically) or the heap (managed by the garbage collector). There is no manual free and no pointer arithmetic.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Mutating method receivers, passing large structs without copying, building linked data structures (trees, lists), and signaling 'optional/absent' via a nil pointer.
foundations.businessImpact: Avoiding large-value copies in hot paths cuts CPU and memory bandwidth, lowering cost at scale; safe (GC-managed) pointers reduce whole classes of crashes versus manual memory management.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Pointers make mutation explicit in signatures (*T vs T), but they introduce nil-dereference risk and shared-mutable-state concerns that must be handled carefully.
foundations.performanceImpact: Passing a pointer is O(1) regardless of the pointed-to size, versus copying a large struct by value. But pointers can force heap allocation (escape) and add GC pressure, so for small values a copy is often cheaper.
commonUseCases: Mutating a caller's value or struct from a function
Pointer receivers for methods that modify state

commonMisconceptions.myth: Go pointers are dangerous like C pointers.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Go has no pointer arithmetic and a garbage collector; you can't fabricate addresses or leak memory the way you can in C.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Passing a pointer is always faster.
commonMisconceptions.reality: For small values, copying is cheap and avoids heap allocation; pointers can cause escapes and GC pressure that cost more.

commonMisconceptions.myth: A nil pointer is the same as a zero value you can read.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Dereferencing a nil pointer panics; you must check for nil before *p.

visualExplorer.title: How `inc(&n)` modifies the caller's variable
visualExplorer.caption: Passing the address lets a by-value function reach back and mutate the original.

steps.name: n lives in main
steps.detail: n := 1 occupies an address, say 0x100, in main's frame.

steps.name: Take its address
steps.detail: &n produces the value 0x100, a *int pointing at n.

steps.name: Call copies the pointer
steps.detail: inc receives a copy of the pointer p — but it still holds 0x100.

steps.name: Dereference and write
steps.detail: *p++ goes to address 0x100 and increments the value there.

steps.name: Caller sees the change
steps.detail: Back in main, n is now 2 because the function wrote to n's actual memory.

interactiveExamples.title: Take an address and write through it
interactiveExamples.explanation: &x gives a pointer to x. Writing *p = 20 changes x itself because p holds x's address.

code.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	x := 10
	p := &x          // p points at x
	fmt.Println(*p)  // read through the pointer: 10
	*p = 20          // write through the pointer
	fmt.Println(x)   // x changed: 20
}

interactiveExamples.title: Edit it: make swap actually swap
interactiveExamples.explanation: Taking ints by value swaps only the copies. Edit swap to take pointers so the caller's variables are exchanged.

checkpoints.explanation: p points at x. *p reads 5; *p = *p + 10 writes 15 back to x's address. So x is now 15.

checkpoints.prompt: Why does this program panic at runtime?
checkpoints.code:
var p *int        // nil pointer
fmt.Println(*p)   // dereference
options: *p dereferences a nil pointer, which panics
Pointers must be initialized with new
checkpoints.explanation: The zero value of a pointer is nil. Dereferencing nil (*p) causes a runtime panic: 'invalid memory address or nil pointer dereference'. Initialize it (p = &x or p = new(int)) before dereferencing, or check for nil.

checkpoints.prompt: Which call lets `inc` modify the caller's n, given `func inc(p *int) { *p++ }`?
checkpoints.explanation: inc expects a *int. &n takes n's address and passes it, so *p++ increments the real n. inc(n) is a type error, *n is invalid (n isn't a pointer), and new(n) isn't valid syntax.

checkpoints.prompt: Allocate a new User and get a pointer to it, initializing Name.
checkpoints.explanation: &User{...} builds the struct and yields a *User you can initialize with fields. User{...} is a value (not a pointer), *User{...} is invalid syntax, and new(T) can't take initial field values.

codeLab.title: Clamp a value in place through a pointer
codeLab.instructions: Implement `Clamp(n *int, lo, hi int)` that, given a pointer to an int, adjusts the pointed-to value so it lies within [lo, hi]: below lo becomes lo, above hi becomes hi, otherwise unchanged. Handle a nil pointer safely by doing nothing.
hints: Check for nil first so you never dereference a nil pointer.
Compare *n against lo and hi, then write the clamped value back through *n.
Only one bound can be violated at a time, so an if/else-if is enough.

debuggingLab.title: Nil pointer dereference panic
debuggingLab.symptom: The program panics with 'invalid memory address or nil pointer dereference'.
debuggingLab.errorAnalysis: var c *Config declares a pointer whose value is nil — no Config exists yet. Writing c.Port implicitly dereferences c (it is (*c).Port), and dereferencing nil panics. You must allocate a Config first.
commonMistakes: Declaring a pointer but never allocating the value it should point to.
Confusing var c *Config (nil pointer) with var c Config (usable zero value).
debuggingLab.fixChallenge: Allocate a Config so c points at real memory before assigning fields.

theory.question: What is a pointer in Go, and what do & and * do?
theory.directAnswer: A pointer holds the memory address of a value; its type is *T. The & operator takes the address of a value (&x yields a *T), and the * operator dereferences a pointer to read or write the value it points to (*p). Go has no pointer arithmetic, and its garbage collector manages the lifetime of pointed-to memory.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A typed address: a *T value that refers to a T stored elsewhere in memory.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: To share and mutate values across function boundaries and to avoid copying large data.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: & computes an address; * follows it. The compiler decides via escape analysis whether the value lives on the stack or heap.

theory.whyImportant: Pointers underpin mutation, method receivers, and efficient data passing — foundational Go knowledge.
theory.realWorldExample: A Save(u *User) function updates fields on the caller's User instead of a throwaway copy.

followUps.question: Does Go have pointer arithmetic?
followUps.answer: No — you cannot add to or subtract from pointers (except via the unsafe package, which is discouraged). This prevents a major class of memory bugs.

followUps.question: Who frees the memory a pointer refers to?
followUps.answer: The garbage collector reclaims it once nothing reachable points to it; there is no manual free.

theory.question: When should you pass a pointer versus a value to a function?
theory.directAnswer: Pass a pointer when the function must modify the caller's value, or when the value is large enough that copying it is wasteful. Pass by value for small, immutable-by-intent data, since copies are cheap and avoid heap allocation and shared-state concerns.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A design choice between sharing an address and copying a value.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Go is pass-by-value; pointers are the explicit opt-in to shared, mutable access.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: A pointer is one word regardless of size; a value copy duplicates all bytes. Pointers may force a heap escape and add GC work.

theory.whyImportant: It directly affects correctness (mutation) and performance (copy cost vs allocation) — a common interview judgment call.
theory.realWorldExample: A 512-byte config struct is passed by pointer in a hot loop to avoid copying it on every call.

followUps.question: What is escape analysis?
followUps.answer: A compiler analysis that decides whether a value can stay on the stack or must move to the heap (e.g., because a pointer to it outlives the function).

followUps.question: Is a slice or map an exception?
followUps.answer: Slices and maps already hold an internal reference, so passing them by value still lets you mutate their underlying data without an explicit pointer.

scenario.question: A service intermittently panics with 'nil pointer dereference' only under certain inputs. How do you diagnose and prevent it?
scenario.directAnswer: Some code path leaves a pointer (or interface, map, or struct field that is a pointer) nil and then dereferences it. Diagnose from the panic's stack trace to find the exact dereference, then guard with nil checks, ensure constructors always initialize pointers, and prefer designs where the zero value is usable. Tests covering the triggering inputs catch it permanently.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A runtime panic from following a nil address.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: A pointer was declared or returned but never pointed at a real value before use.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: The stack trace names the file/line of the dereference; from there you trace where the pointer should have been set.

scenario.whyImportant: Nil dereferences are among the most common Go production crashes.
scenario.realWorldExample: An error path returns (nil, nil) by mistake; the caller dereferences the nil result, panicking only when that path is hit.

followUps.question: How can the type system help avoid this?
followUps.answer: Return zero-value structs instead of pointers where 'absent' isn't meaningful, or use the (value, ok) / (value, error) patterns so callers must check before using.

coding.question: Implement `func Reverse(head *Node) *Node` that reverses a singly linked list, where `type Node struct { Val int; Next *Node }`.
coding.thoughtProcess: Walk the list with three pointers — prev, cur, next — flipping each node's Next to point backward. Save next before rewiring so we don't lose the rest of the list. Return prev, which ends up at the old tail (the new head).
coding.lineByLine: prev starts nil because the original head becomes the new tail (its Next must be nil). For each node we stash next, point cur.Next at prev to reverse the link, then move both prev and cur forward. When cur reaches nil the list is fully reversed and prev points at the new head.
coding.timeComplexity: O(n) — one pass over the list.

followUps.question: Why save next before setting cur.Next = prev?
followUps.answer: Setting cur.Next = prev overwrites the forward link, so without saving next you'd lose access to the remaining nodes.

followUps.question: How would a recursive version differ in space?
followUps.answer: Recursion uses O(n) stack space for the call frames, versus O(1) for the iterative approach.

productionDeepDive.architecture: Make mutation explicit in signatures: take *T when you intend to modify, take T when you don't. Use constructors (NewX) that always return fully-initialized pointers to avoid nil-field surprises.
productionDeepDive.performance: Profile before reaching for pointers: copying small structs is often cheaper than the heap allocation a pointer can trigger. Use go build -gcflags=-m to inspect escape analysis.
productionDeepDive.concurrency: A shared pointer means shared mutable state; protect concurrent access with a mutex or channels, and run tests under -race to catch data races.
productionDeepDive.reliability: Treat every pointer that might be unset as nilable: check before dereferencing, and design zero values to be usable so 'forgot to initialize' bugs can't occur.
productionDeepDive.observability: Nil-dereference panics print a clear stack trace; capture panics with recover at goroutine boundaries and log the trace to pinpoint the offending dereference.
productionDeepDive.security: Avoid the unsafe package unless absolutely necessary; bypassing Go's pointer safety can introduce memory-corruption vulnerabilities.

caseStudies.problem: Excessive heap allocations from passing everything by pointer increased GC time.
caseStudies.solution: Passed small structs by value and reserved pointers for large or mutable data, guided by escape-analysis output.
caseStudies.lessons: Pointers are not automatically faster — let profiling and escape analysis decide.

keyTakeaways: A pointer (*T) holds the address of a value; & takes an address and * reads/writes through it.
Pass a pointer when a function must mutate the caller's value or to avoid copying large data.
The zero value of a pointer is nil; dereferencing nil panics, so check before *p.
Go has no pointer arithmetic and a garbage collector, making pointers far safer than C's — but they can add heap allocation and GC pressure.
